title: Diwali at the ruins
hookLine: months later the Sikhs gathered at Amritsar again and began to rebuild

lines: THE SEASON OF LAMPS COMES ROUND.
cards: Lamps along a broken wall. That's the scene tradition keeps. The Harmandir is rubble, and the pool around it has been fouled and filled.
The army that did it is still in Punjab, and the families who survived the great killing earlier that year are still burying people.
Then the season of Diwali comes round, the festival of lamps, and Sikhs start arriving in Amritsar. Not a few. Riders, families, whole bands, coming to the ruins on the day they have always come.

teach.h: DIWALI: THE DAY OF RELEASE AND HOMECOMING.
teach.b: Why Diwali? For Sikhs, Diwali at Amritsar had long been a time to gather, as Vaisakhi was in spring.
It's tied in Sikh memory to Guru Hargobind coming home to Amritsar after being released from prison, the day many Sikhs now call Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release.
So the date already meant coming back to the Guru's city after a time of captivity. They came on purpose, on the day that means homecoming. Then, what they found: no building to gather in.

teach.h: NO BUILDING, AND THEY GATHERED ANYWAY.
teach.b: Tradition says they gathered anyway, at the place itself, because the place was never only the bricks. And what they did: they began clearing. Cleaning the pool.

teach.h: CLEARING THE POOL, THE FIRST STONES.
teach.b: Taking the first stones of a new beginning.

teach.h: THE LORD STANDS UP TO FINISH THE WORK.
teach.b: Guru Arjan's hymn about the pool, the one this path heard four days ago, comes back here, in paraphrase: the Lord himself stood up to complete the work of the saints.
Some Sikhs sing it when new work begins, and it's easy to hear why it fit that autumn. The work wasn't theirs alone.
Tradition also says Abdali's army, still in Punjab, fell on the gathering that season and there was fighting at Amritsar, so this was no quiet festival. Rebuilding the Harmandir fully took years.
But the beginning was a crowd of people with lamps at a ruin, refusing to let the day pass unmarked.

how: Sikhs celebrate Diwali as Bandi Chhor Divas, and at Amritsar the Harmandir Sahib and its pool are lit with lamps; the story of gathering at the ruins is told in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks.

games.why: tradition says they came to Amritsar and began clearing and rebuilding. the place mattered more than the walls.

practice: Sit with something that broke, a plan, a habit, a friendship, and don't try to fix the whole of it; the Sikhs at Amritsar didn't rebuild a temple that night, they lit lamps and moved some stones.
Ask only what the first stone is, one message, one drawer cleared, one page, and stay with it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Diwali, the festival of lamps. After the Harmandir was destroyed, tradition says the Sikhs gathered at Amritsar for it anyway, and began clearing the pool and rebuilding. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for Diwali, the festival of lamps, which Sikhs keep as Bandi Chhor Divas.

carryVoice: Your line: begin again. Nobody rebuilds a temple in a night. Day eight hundred sixty-seven, lamps lit.
